METIS can be configured end-to-end with [Hydra](https://hydra.cc). You don't
need to touch Python to change models, datasets or training settings — you
compose and override Hydra configs instead. The configs call the same package
functions used in the Python examples.

## Hydra basics

Hydra's configuration files are simple text-based [YAML](https://yaml.org/about/)
files. For example, part of a training configuration might look like this:

```yaml
training:
  steps: 1000
  learning_rate: 0.001
```

Once read by the program, these values can be accessed as
`config.training.steps` and `config.training.learning_rate`. You can change
settings without editing the program itself.

Rather than putting every setting in one file, Hydra lets us compose a
configuration from smaller files. METIS installs these with the package:

```text
metis/conf/
├── config.yaml
├── dataset/
│   ├── example.yaml
│   └── parquet.yaml
├── model/
│   ├── mlp.yaml
│   ├── transformer.yaml
│   ├── flow_matching.yaml
│   └── itarflow.yaml
└── training/
    └── default.yaml
```

The main `config.yaml` chooses one file from each group using a `defaults` list:

```yaml
defaults:
  - dataset: example
  - model: mlp
  - training: default
  - _self_
```

This loads `dataset/example.yaml`, `model/mlp.yaml` and `training/default.yaml`.
`_self_` means that values written in the main config are applied after those
defaults. The resulting configuration combines the dataset, model and training
settings into one experiment.

You can inspect the complete configuration without training:

```bash
uv run metis train --cfg job
```

When running a job, override a group or an individual value on the command line:

```bash
uv run metis train model=transformer training.steps=1000
```

Here `model=transformer` selects a different YAML file, while
`training.steps=1000` changes one value. The dataset remains the bundled SIRDS
example. To change a setting within the MLP configuration:

```bash
uv run metis train model=mlp model.model_options.hidden_dim=128
```

These commands work from your own project directory. The `metis` command is
installed with the package; it does not need a `train.py` file in your project.
`uv run metis-train` is an equivalent entry point.

::: {.callout-tip}
Hydra has many more features not mentioned here. The
[Hydra tutorials](https://hydra.cc/docs/tutorials/intro/) explain configuration
groups, composition and command-line overrides in more detail.
:::

## Writing a config for our data

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
graph TD
    A[Dataset config] --> D[Experiment config]
    B[Model config] --> D
    C[Training config] --> D
    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff,stroke:none
    style B fill:#7b61ff,color:#fff,stroke:none
    style C fill:#548c56,color:#fff,stroke:none
    style D fill:#e06c75,color:#fff,stroke:none
```

For our first experiment we can keep the model and training defaults and add
one dataset config. In [preparing data](preparing-data.qmd), we saved our SIRDS
simulations as `sirds_data.parquet`. Create a `configs/dataset` directory in
your project and save the following as `sirds.yaml`:

```yaml
_target_: metis.SimulationDataset.from_parquet
path: sirds_data.parquet
inputs:
  - I_0
  - beta
  - gamma
  - omega
  - mu
outputs:
  - S_t
  - I_t
  - R_t
  - D_t
groups: null
time: t
replicate: rep
```

`_target_` tells Hydra to call `SimulationDataset.from_parquet`; the other
entries are its arguments. `inputs` are the static parameters we condition on
and `outputs` are the trajectories we want to predict. With `groups: null`,
replicates with the same input parameters are kept together when splitting the
bank. If your bank has a separate scenario identifier, supply its column name
in a list, for example `groups: [scenario]`.

Your project now contains:

```text
my-surrogate/
├── pyproject.toml
├── uv.lock
├── sirds_data.parquet
└── configs/
    └── dataset/
        └── sirds.yaml
```

Tell Hydra where to find this additional configuration:

```bash
uv run metis train --config-dir "$PWD/configs" dataset=sirds model=mlp training.steps=1000
```

Hydra combines your dataset file with the installed model and training defaults.
You do not need to copy or edit the package's configuration files. Relative data
paths are resolved from the directory where you run the command. For a quick
check without creating YAML, the same dataset can be selected with overrides:

```bash
uv run metis train dataset=parquet dataset.path=sirds_data.parquet 'dataset.inputs=[I_0,beta,gamma,omega,mu]' 'dataset.outputs=[S_t,I_t,R_t,D_t]'
```

Each job saves its resolved configuration, trained model, training history and
evaluation results under `outputs/`. With plotting support installed, add
`plot.enabled=true` to save a comparison figure.

## Trying several settings {#sweeps}

Hydra's `--multirun` option runs combinations of settings:

```bash
uv run metis train --multirun model=mlp,transformer training.learning_rate=0.001,0.0003 evaluation.partition=validation
```

This runs four experiments. Compare validation results when choosing settings,
and keep the test partition for the final evaluation. The
[sweeping tutorial](../sweeping/overview.qmd) develops this further.

With the optional W&B dependency, add `wandb.enabled=true` to track a run;
[Weights & Biases](../sweeping/wandb.qmd) explains setup and tracking.

Next, [train our first surrogates](training.qmd) and compare their SIRDS predictions.
